title: ICD-10, CPT, and HCPCS Coding Fundamentals
summary: Three coding systems — ICD-10-CM/PCS, CPT, and HCPCS — work together to describe diagnoses and procedures for billing purposes.
objectives: Distinguish between ICD-10-CM, ICD-10-PCS, CPT, and HCPCS Level II codes
Explain how diagnosis and procedure codes work together on a claim
Describe the role of DRGs in inpatient hospital billing

concepts.definition: International Classification of Diseases, 10th Revision, Clinical Modification — used to report diagnoses in all care settings; ~72,000 codes
Procedure Coding System — used by hospitals to report inpatient procedures; ~87,000 codes organized by body system and approach
Current Procedural Terminology — AMA-maintained codes for physician services, outpatient procedures, and ancillary services; updated annually
Healthcare Common Procedure Coding System — CMS-maintained codes for drugs, supplies, DME, and ambulance services not covered by CPT
Diagnosis-Related Group — CMS payment category grouping similar inpatient diagnoses; determines the fixed payment for a Medicare inpatient stay
Complication or Comorbidity / Major Complication or Comorbidity — secondary diagnoses that increase DRG weight and reimbursement when documented

content_blocks.body:
For outpatient/professional claims, CPT procedure codes paired with ICD-10-CM diagnosis codes determine payment under Medicare's Physician Fee Schedule (PFS) or payer fee schedules. Medical necessity requires that the diagnosis code supports the procedure.

For hospital inpatient claims, ICD-10-CM diagnosis codes and ICD-10-PCS procedure codes are grouped into a DRG. CMS pays a fixed rate per DRG regardless of actual resource use (with outlier adjustments for extreme cases). The principal diagnosis, complications (CC/MCC), and procedures all affect DRG assignment and payment.
content_blocks.heading: How Codes Drive Payment

content_blocks.body: Documenting and coding secondary diagnoses as CCs or MCCs can increase DRG payment by 15–35%. Examples: Documenting 'acute blood loss anemia' vs. 'anemia' — the former may qualify as a CC. Clinical documentation improvement (CDI) programs focus specifically on capturing these diagnoses when clinically supported.
